panels.rationale: Sagittal MRI of the lumbar spine in a patient with myxoid liposarcoma shows an L2 vertebral body metastasis with abnormal T1 signal, as described in the caption and in-text mentions. Bone metastasis is a recognized but less common manifestation.
panels.attribution_text: Noble et al. Imaging of skeletal metastases in myxoid liposarcoma.. Sarcoma 2010. doi:10.1155/2010/262361. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: The MRI scan shows homogeneous isointense signal relative to skeletal muscle on T1-weighted images throughout L2 vertebra. The cortex is intact.
in_text_mentions: Patient 1 was diagnosed with MRCL in a paravertebral muscle which was excised with a marginal excision. He relapsed locally one year later and at this time an MRI scan showed tumour in the L2 vertebral body (Figure 1). Low signal was seen within the body of L2 on T1 corresponding to high signal on T2 in keeping with an intraosseous metastasis. A staging CT scan was performed showing no significant abnormality on bone windows at L2 or elsewhere (Figure 2). Plain X-rays and bone scan were not performed. The patient went on to receive chemotherapy with a good response but has since progressed.

in_text_mentions: The final histopathology report showed soft tissue sarcoma with the presence of plump spindle cells in a myxoid matrix with the presence of numerous branching blood vessels and capillary channels. There are numerous lipoblast‐like cells with the presence of a scalloped nucleus and clear multiloculated cytoplasm. Numerous mature adipocytes were also identified. Mitosis was less than 10 per high power field. The tumor was positive for S100 and MDM2, and negative for MCV4, EMA, BCL2, CD99, and CD56, suggestive of well‐differentiated myxoid liposarcoma (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: B-mode ultrasound panel from a real patient with captioned myxoid liposarcoma, showing a heterogeneous mass with hypoechoic foci. B: Color Doppler ultrasound panel captioned as myxoid liposarcoma, showing poor vascularity with low arterial peak systolic velocity. C: Power Doppler ultrasound panel captioned as myxoid liposarcoma, demonstrating mild central vascularity.
panels.attribution_text: Ferenc et al. Multiparametric US and MRI Features of Femoral Myxoid Liposarcoma-Case Report and Literature Review.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2026. doi:10.3390/diagnostics16091286. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: B-mode, color, and power Doppler images of MLS: (A) On B-mode, MLS presented as a heterogeneous mass with hypoechoic foci; (B) on color Doppler, MLS was poorly vascularized with a low arterial peak systolic velocity of 13 cm/s (not shown on image); (C) on power Doppler, MLS also demonstrated mild central vascularity.
in_text_mentions: ed, expansive mass measuring 6.8 × 5.2 × 9.1 cm, with heterogeneous echogenicity and no signs of infiltration into adjacent structures. On color and power Doppler evaluation, the mass was poorly vascularized with low-flow velocity arteries and veins (peak systolic velocity of arterial flow was 13 cm/s) (Figure 1). B-flow imaging showed that the mass was moderately vascularized with low-flow blood vessels. On strain elastography, the mass demonstrated heterogeneous stiffness but was predominantly soft (2D shear-wave elastography (2D SWE) was not available at the time of examination) (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Patient orbital tumor tissue shown by low-power H&E; article title and in-text identify the neoplasm as myxoid liposarcoma, and the overview demonstrates a malignant adipose-origin neoplasm. B: Patient orbital myxoid liposarcoma tissue; H&E shows the classic myxoid stroma and branching/chicken-wire capillary network described in the caption. C: Higher-power patient tumor H&E showing signet-ring lipoblasts, a characteristic histologic feature of myxoid liposarcoma. D: Patient tumor immunohistochemistry showing S-100 protein expression; in-text confirms positivity in the myxoid liposarcoma cells. E: Patient tumor immunohistochemistry showing vimentin expression, consistent with the article's reported myxoid liposarcoma immunophenotype. F: Patient tumor immunohistochemistry showing apparent CD-57 expression, as stated in the caption and in-text for this myxoid liposarcoma.
panels.attribution_text: Benavides-Huerto et al. Primary Orbital Myxoid Liposarcoma.. Medical sciences (Basel, Switzerland) 2023. doi:10.3390/medsci11040072. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological analysis of the case. (A) Overview of the tumor neoplasm (H&E, 1×). (B) The neoplasm has a marked myxoid appearance with numerous branching blood vessels (H&E, 5×). (C) Signet ring cells and perineural invasion are evident at higher magnification (H&E, 10×). (D) Immunohistological analysis of S-100 protein (40×). (E) Immunohistological analysis of vimentin (40×). (F) Immunohistological analysis of CD-57 in tumor tissue (40×).
in_text_mentions: Histological analysis revealed a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm of adipose origin (Figure 2A). This neoplasm consisted of a mixture of adipose “signet ring” cells, some with stellate nuclei and others with a more spindle-shaped appearance (Figure 2B,C). Notably, these cells were positive for S-100 protein and vimentin and were embedded in a myxoid stroma (Figure 2D,E).
Furthermore, the lesion had a network of branching blood vessels and showed apparent CD-57 expression (Figure 2F).

in_text_mentions: in a postmenopausal woman with a known history of malignancy and a family history of breast cancer, a BI-RADS Category 4 was assigned with recommendation for definitive tissue diagnosis via ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy [9]. The tissue specimen from the ultrasound-guided biopsy (Figure 3) showed liposarcoma with high-grade round cell components in the majority of the tissue (Figure 4). Rearrangement of DDIT3 (DNA Damage Inducible Transcript 3), a transcription factor associated with myxoid liposarcoma, was detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), supporting the diagnosis.

panels.rationale: Single ultrasound image from a human patient with retroperitoneal myxoid liposarcoma; caption and in-text description support a solid heterogeneous mass. Retroperitoneal location is a less common presentation, so classified as variant.

in_text_mentions: Physical examination showed a palpable mass especially extended in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. plate_findings.evidence: The cut surface of the tumor was gray, friable, honeycomb-shaped, and muculent

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Gross specimen photograph of a large grey neoplasm from a patient with pancreatic metastasis of extremity myxoid liposarcoma. The panel is a real patient-derived gross image, but the external surface appearance is nonspecific; disease attribution rests on the article title and case context. B: Gross cut-surface photograph of a myxoid liposarcoma metastasis to the pancreas. The caption describes a gray, friable, honeycomb-shaped, muculent cut surface, corresponding to the gelatinous/myxoid cut surface characteristic of myxoid liposarcoma. The pancreatic metastatic site is an uncommon presentation, hence variant.

(A,B) A heterogeneous hypoechoic mass measuring approximately 7.8 cm × 7.0 cm was observed in the upper middle part of the left kidney with indistinct borders. Color Doppler flow imaging (CDFI) revealed the presence of grade II flow signal within the mass. (C,D) Additionally, a cystic solid mass measuring approximately 4.8 cm × 4.4 cm was identified in the posterior part of the pancreas, immediately adjacent to the superior pole of the left kidney. CDFI indicated the presence of grade I blood flow signal within the mass. (E) The arterial phase transverse CT image depicted a protruding mass in the upper middle part of the left kidney, exhibiting extrarenal growth (long arrows), blurring of the perirenal fat gap, and significant enhancement (76 HU). (F) A volume rending (VR) image demonstrated abundant blood supply to the mass, with multiple branches of the left renal artery entering the lesion. (G,H) Coronal and sagittal images obtained from the venous phase displayed invasion of the pancreas by the left kidney mass (98 HU).

in_text_mentions: At the age of 61, whole-body MRI revealed a cardiac lesion with high signal intensity on T2-weighted fat-suppression imaging. A retrospective review of the MRI scan taken 6 months earlier confirmed the presence of the lesion. Cardiac MRI was performed to further evaluate the lesion, diagnosing metastatic tumors in the left ventricular epicardium and myocardium. Tumor resection was planned (Fig. 1). Echocardiography revealed an occupying lesion with a cystic appearance at the apex and within the ventricular septum (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Cardiac MRI panel from a case report titled misdiagnosis of pericardial myxoid liposarcoma; T1-hypointense pericardial lesion marked with a red asterisk. The pericardial location is atypical for myxoid liposarcoma. B: T2-hyperintense pericardial lesion in the same case; supports myxoid liposarcoma imaging features in an atypical cardiac/pericardial location. C: DWI/ADC hyperintense pericardial mass; no exact vocabulary term for restricted diffusion, but enhancement pattern and article context support myxoid liposarcoma. D: LGE MRI showing progressive internal fill-in of the pericardial mass, consistent with the reported pericardial myxoid liposarcoma, although atypical in location.
panels.attribution_text: Wang et al. Case report and diagnostic implications of misdiagnosis of pericardial myxoid liposarcoma by multimodal imaging.. Frontiers in cardiovascular medicine 2025. doi:10.3389/fcvm.2025.1685844. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) findings, including late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). (A) Cardiac MRI revealing a space-occupying lesion within the pericardium, lateral to the left ventricle, suggestive of a hemangioma. The findings also included a thickened pericardium with a small amount of effusion. An ovoid lesion with abnormal signal intensity (indicated by *), measuring approximately 37 × 62 × 61 mm, was identified in this location. The lesion appeared hypointense on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), and a discernible fat plane was present between the lesion and the lateral wall of the left ventricle. (B) Lesion appeared hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI). (C) Lesion appeared hyperintense on both diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps. Following contrast administration, the lesion demonstrated marked heterogeneous enhancement, with progressive internal fill-in observed on delayed scans. (D) Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) demonstrating progressive internal fill-in.
in_text_mentions: MRI (Figure 3) revealed enlargement of both atria and an oval abnormal lesion (∼37 mm × 62 mm × 61 mm) located laterally within the pericardium; the lesion showed high signal intensity on T2WI, low signal on T1WI, and high signal on DWI and ADC sequences. The lesion exhibited marked heterogeneous enhancement with delayed inward contrast filling, suggesting a possible hemangioma. Early (30–90 s) and late (3–10 min) postcontrast phases demonstrated progressive internal fill-in with delayed enhancement (LGE). Notably, T2-weighted fat-suppression imaging revealed no fat tissue-related signal loss.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a real-patient B-flow ultrasound image of a femoral myxoid liposarcoma (caption: 'B-flow imaging showed MLS to be moderately vascularized'), with a grayscale US image and a color-coded vascularity overlay showing moderate low-flow vascularity. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title and panel-specific captioned manifestation. B: Panel B is a real-patient strain elastography ultrasound image (grayscale image plus color elastogram) of the same femoral myxoid liposarcoma. The caption states the mass was 'predominantly a soft mass, resembling an elastography score of 1 according to Griffith, which is a characteristic for benign masses', an unusual (atypical) elastographic appearance for MLS; disease attribution rests on the disease-focused title and in-text description of this MLS mass.
panels.attribution_text: Ferenc et al. Multiparametric US and MRI Features of Femoral Myxoid Liposarcoma-Case Report and Literature Review.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2026. doi:10.3390/diagnostics16091286. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: B-flow imaging and strain elastography of MLS: (A) B-flow imaging showed MLS to be moderately vascularized; (B) strain elastography showed MLS to be predominantly a soft mass, resembling an elastography score of 1 according to Griffith [6], which is a characteristic for benign masses (strain ratio and E/B ratio were not measured due to technical limitations and 2D SWE was not available at the time of examination).
in_text_mentions: ed, expansive mass measuring 6.8 × 5.2 × 9.1 cm, with heterogeneous echogenicity and no signs of infiltration into adjacent structures. On color and power Doppler evaluation, the mass was poorly vascularized with low-flow velocity arteries and veins (peak systolic velocity of arterial flow was 13 cm/s) (Figure 1). B-flow imaging showed that the mass was moderately vascularized with low-flow blood vessels. On strain elastography, the mass demonstrated heterogeneous stiffness but was predominantly soft (2D shear-wave elastography (2D SWE) was not available at the time of examination) (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Gross photograph of a resected cardiac tumor; the article and caption identify it as myxoid liposarcoma metastatic to the heart. Cardiac metastasis is an unusual presentation. B: H&E histology shows classic myxoid liposarcoma features: myxoid matrix and plexiform/chicken-wire capillary network, explicitly described in the caption and text. C: H&E section shows myxoid liposarcoma invading myocardium, as stated in the caption and in-text description. Myocardial invasion is an unusual manifestation. D: H&E section shows myxoid liposarcoma invading myocardium, supported by the caption and text. Myocardial invasion is an unusual manifestation.

in_text_mentions: . These branches were clipped and divided. As the dissection continued along the tumor margins, most of the myocardium was easily separated, because the tumor was white, elastic, and firm, did not invade the surrounding tissue, and had well-defined borders. However, at 2 or 3 locations, mainly in the center of the tumor, the tumor continuously extended deep into the interventricular septum. After completing dissection in these areas (Fig. 3A), the surface portion of the tumor was quickly submitted for intraoperative pathological examination, which confirmed the diagnosis of myxoid liposarcoma.

Histologic examination of the resected specimen revealed a proliferation of bland stellate tumor cells embedded in a myxoid matrix with a prominent plexiform capillary network (Fig. 3B). No mitotic activity or pleomorphism was observed. These histologic features were consistent with those of a low-grade myxoid liposarcoma. The neoplastic cells invaded the cardiac muscle fibers (Fig. 3C and 3D).

panels.figure_caption: MRI imaging of a massive right thigh tumor. (A) shows a coronal T2-weighted image, and (B) shows an axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image. in_text_mentions: muscle of the thigh. No hematoma was found. The abnormal mucinous tissue was removed, and the thigh wound was sutured, leaving a drain. The procedure was uncomplicated, but the lesion was not removed in its entirety due to deep infiltration of the quadriceps muscle. In magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of both thighs after surgical treatment, in the proximal part of the thigh, in the long adductor muscle, a nodular lesion measuring 138 × 89 × 71 mm having numerous internal septa was visible. The lesion was heterogeneous, with an increased signal in T2-weighted and PD-weighted images (Figure 3).

rst plan was to prepare the patient for a specific expert orthopedic oncology operation; however, after seeing the NGS and FISH results and changing the diagnosis to high-grade myxoid liposarcoma, an oncological committee review (tumor board review) was performed. This tumor board always includes a surgeon specializing in the relevant area, a clinical oncologist, a geneticist, a radiation therapist, and a chemotherapist. The decision was to perform neoadjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy before the operation (Figure 3). The patient gave written consent to publish the description of her case.

in_text_mentions: tic body. The cut surface of the tumor had a myxoidal appearance (Figure 3). Pathological findings revealed round‐to‐stellate atypical cells proliferating within the myxoid stroma, infiltrating the pancreatic parenchyma and adipose tissue. Most areas showed cystic changes, and a few lipoblasts were observed. No round cell components were observed (Figure 4). Immunohistochemical analysis was positive for DDIT3 and negative for MDM2 and CDK4. Accordingly, the tumor was diagnosed as a pancreatic metastasis of a previously resected MLS in the right thigh. A pathological R0 resection was performed.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Coronal T2 MRI panel of a histologically/imaging-confirmed myxoid liposarcoma of the leg, showing the classic T2-hyperintense intramuscular mass with hypointense septa; caption and in-text explicitly attribute the imaging to myxoid liposarcoma. B: Coronal T1 MRI panel showing the T1-hypointense intramuscular myxoid liposarcoma, consistent with the caption and in-text attribution to myxoid liposarcoma. C: Axial fat-saturated post-contrast T1 MRI of the same myxoid liposarcoma showing contrast enhancement; the enhancing septal/reticular pattern is a recognized myxoid liposarcoma feature. D: Diffusion-weighted MRI panel of the same myxoid liposarcoma showing irregular diffusion restriction, as stated in the caption and in-text.
panels.attribution_text: Montana et al. Myxoid liposarcoma of the leg: a case report.. BJR case reports 2026. doi:10.1093/bjrcr/uaaf055. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: MRI of myxoid liposarcoma. (A) Coronal T2-weighted image; (B) Coronal T1-weighted image; (C) Axial T1 fat-saturated post-contrast image; (D) Diffusion-weighted image. The bulky solid mass shows oval morphology, a predominantly hyperintense signal on T2 with thin hypointense septa, a hypointense signal on T1, irregular diffusion restriction, and conspicuous post-contrast enhancement.
in_text_mentions: Due to the size and characteristics MRI were performed and revealed a large, heterogeneous mass within the intermuscular fascial planes of the anterior compartment of the leg with high signal intensity on T2 images and areas of low signal intensity due to the myxoid material. The imaging indicated minimal fat content, resulting in low T1 signal, with some hyperintensity spots, aligning with the diagnosis of myxoid liposarcoma. We also performed DWI and T1 Fat-Sat (FS) + contrast sequences showing respectively restriction and contrast uptake of the lesion (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photograph of a large painless thigh mass in a case report of myxoid liposarcoma; the mass is a visible clinical manifestation but nonspecific. B: Axial T1-weighted MRI shows an intramuscular sartorius mass in a myxoid liposarcoma case; T1 iso-intensity is a less typical but recognized appearance. C: Axial T2-weighted MRI shows a hyperintense intramuscular mass, characteristic of the myxoid matrix in myxoid liposarcoma. D: Axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted fat-suppressed MRI shows the intramuscular mass with partial enhancement, consistent with the reported myxoid tumor.

panels.figure_caption: Findings on primary encounter. A mobile, elastic, and firm tumor (16 × 13 cm) was evident in the distal third of the right thigh (A). Axial MRI of the right thigh revealed a soft tissue mass inside the right sartorius. Compared to the surrounding muscle, the lesion was iso‐intense on T1‐weighted imaging (B). The lesion was hyperintense on T2‐weighted imaging, and there was no communication with the femoral vessels (C). The lesion was partially enhanced with gadolinium on T1‐weighted imaging with fat suppression (D). These findings suggested an extensive myxomatous tumor.

(B) Microscopic histopathological findings: spindle cell tumor with relatively uniform, short-spindle cells exhibiting cellular atypia and conspicuous mitotic figures, abundant myxoid stroma, and rich vascularity. Immunohistochemical staining results: (C) vimentin (+); (D) MDM2 (weak+); and (E) MUC4 (weak+).

in_text_mentions: 3-year-old man presented with an abdominal wall mass of nine months duration, increasing rapidly in size without any other associated symptoms. On physical examination, the mass was located in the left abdominal wall. It was soft and mobile, and had a diameter of 9 cm. An abdominal MRI with intravenous contrast revealed a heterogeneous mass in the left rectus abdominis muscle tumor lesion enhanced early and continuously in the late phase, measuring 88 x 65 x 52 mm (Figure 1). A thoracic and abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, which did not reveal any distant metastasis.

panels.figure_caption: There is a right-sided paraspinal metastatic lesion. The bone windows on CT scan show very subtle lytic change in the vertebral body of L2 which was not considered significant at the time of reporting.
in_text_mentions: Patient 1 was diagnosed with MRCL in a paravertebral muscle which was excised with a marginal excision. He relapsed locally one year later and at this time an MRI scan showed tumour in the L2 vertebral body (Figure 1). Low signal was seen within the body of L2 on T1 corresponding to high signal on T2 in keeping with an intraosseous metastasis. A staging CT scan was performed showing no significant abnormality on bone windows at L2 or elsewhere (Figure 2). Plain X-rays and bone scan were not performed. The patient went on to receive chemotherapy with a good response but has since progressed.

The cut-off values of the highest sensitivity and specificity were determined by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. For example, the cut-off values of PHH3-positive tumor

Ki-67 was measured by the same method with PHH3 for comparison (Fig. 1). The cut-off value of the Ki-67 index was determined to be 19% based on the ROC curve (Fig. 2B). in_text_mentions: At the age of 61, whole-body MRI revealed a cardiac lesion with high signal intensity on T2-weighted fat-suppression imaging. A retrospective review of the MRI scan taken 6 months earlier confirmed the presence of the lesion. Cardiac MRI was performed to further evaluate the lesion, diagnosing metastatic tumors in the left ventricular epicardium and myocardium. Tumor resection was planned (Fig. 1). Echocardiography revealed an occupying lesion with a cystic appearance at the apex and within the ventricular septum (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a precontrast axial abdominal CT from a case report of myxoid liposarcoma of the sigmoid mesocolon. The article title identifies the disease, and the caption gives a specific CT manifestation: a cystic portion with mean density of 10 HU. The image is a real patient CT, not a diagram or third-party image. The low-attenuation/cystic appearance is a recognized CT feature of myxoid liposarcoma, though the mesenteric location is a variant presentation. B: Panel B is the postcontrast axial abdominal CT from the same case report of myxoid liposarcoma of the sigmoid mesocolon. It shows stable low attenuation of the cystic portion and enhancing septations described in the in-text mentions. These are specific CT manifestations supporting disease attribution together with the disease-focused article title. The image is a real patient CT and is not third-party material.

in_text_mentions: ending anteriorly to abdominal wall of right upper quadrant and winding the entire distal right kidney without findings of neoplastic infiltration. The tumor displaced the small bowel to the left and the right kidney to the anterior and pushed the uterus to the high quadrant of the abdomen. The mass was well defined from surrounding structures and showed heterogeneous attenuation (Figure 2). Other organs including liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen were within the limit. Abdominal and pelvic magnetic resonance image (MRI) confirmed a retroperitoneal mass close to the right distal kidney.

plate_findings.evidence: large mild heterogeneously enhancing mixed attenuating extratesticular lesion ... with internal soft tissue and fat attenuating areas ... lipomatous part of the tumour of right spermatic cord (white arrow in image A)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Contrast-enhanced CT coronal section of a human patient from a case report titled 'Giant Paratesticular Myxoid Liposarcoma'; the caption identifies the lipomatous spermatic cord tumour (white arrow) causing displacement of the right testis and compression of the left hemiscrotum (arrowhead), consistent with a myxoid liposarcoma manifestation. B: Contrast-enhanced CT sagittal section of the same human patient's paratesticular mass, captioned as the lipomatous tumour of the right spermatic cord (white arrow), from a case report of giant paratesticular myxoid liposarcoma.
panels.attribution_text: Arutperumselvi et al. Giant Paratesticular Myxoid Liposarcoma: A Case Report of a Rare Entity.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.56859. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: CECT abdomen coronal section (A) and sagittal section (B) showing a large mild heterogeneously enhancing mixed attenuating extratesticular lesion measuring approximately 12.7 x 10.9 x 9.3 cm with internal soft tissue and fat attenuating areas and a few peripheral punctate & chalky calcifications seen involving and expanding the right hemi-scrotum with lipomatous part of the tumour of right spermatic cord (white arrow in image A, white arrow in image B). The lesion is seen causing inferior and peripheral displacement of the right testis and significant compression and cranial displacement of the left hemi-scrotum and testis (white arrow head). CECT - Contrast-enhanced computed tomography
in_text_mentions: CECT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large heterogeneously enhancing mixed attenuating extratesticular lesion (~ 12.7 x 10.9 x 9.3 cm) with internal soft tissue and fat attenuating areas and peripheral punctate & chalky calcifications were evident in the right hemi-scrotum, along with lipomatous hypertrophy of right paratesticular tissue (spermatic cord). This mass lesion was causing inferior and peripheral displacement of the right testis and significant compression and cranial displacement of the left hemi-scrotum and testis, as can be seen in Figures 2, 3A, 3B.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial contrast-enhanced CT slice (top-left of the 2x2 montage) showing the large heterogeneous abdominopelvic mass of the reported bladder myxoid liposarcoma, as described in the caption and in-text mentions (21.7 x 15.4 x 15 cm ill-defined heterogeneous mass with fat component and hemorrhage). panels.rationale: Single-panel grayscale ultrasound from a case report titled 'Giant Paratesticular Myxoid Liposarcoma', showing a large heteroechoic solid scrotal/paratesticular mass with hyperechoic areas, matching the captioned manifestation of the disease. The paratesticular location is an uncommon site for myxoid liposarcoma (hence variant). No age, ethnicity or skin assessment is provided in the caption or in-text mentions.
panels.attribution_text: Arutperumselvi et al. Giant Paratesticular Myxoid Liposarcoma: A Case Report of a Rare Entity.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.56859. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Scrotal ultrasound showed a large heteroechoic solid mass (white arrow) measuring approximately 9.9 x 9.4 x 8.7 cm, with hyperechoic areas seen expanding the right hemi-scrotal sac. Both testicles were seen separately; however, the testicular origin of the mass lesion could not be confirmed, necessitating cross-sectional imaging.
in_text_mentions: , stool routine, ESR, β-human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, mycobacterium tuberculosis antibody Ig-G, liver and kidney function tests, and chest x-ray were conducted. All these investigations yielded no specific abnormalities, contributing to the challenge of diagnosing the scrotal mass. Despite the absence of abnormalities in these baseline assessments, imaging modalities, including USG and CECT were performed to characterize the scrotal mass. USG revealed a large heteroechoic solid mass (~9.9 x 9.4 x 8.7 cm) with hyperechoic areas seen expanding the right hemiscrotal sac (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: CECT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large heterogeneously enhancing mixed attenuating extratesticular lesion (~ 12.7 x 10.9 x 9.3 cm) with internal soft tissue and fat attenuating areas and peripheral punctate & chalky calcifications were evident in the right hemi-scrotum, along with lipomatous hypertrophy of right paratesticular tissue (spermatic cord). This mass lesion was causing inferior and peripheral displacement of the right testis and significant compression and cranial displacement of the left hemi-scrotum and testis, as can be seen in Figures 2, 3A, 3B.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: CECT of primary right atrial myxoid liposarcoma; rare cardiac location. B: CECT showing retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, consistent with metastatic myxoid liposarcoma per article title; no direct caption attribution. C: FDG PET showing primary right atrial myxoid liposarcoma; rare cardiac location. D: Coronal FDG PET showing primary right atrial myxoid liposarcoma; rare cardiac location. E: FDG PET showing enlarged lymph nodes, consistent with metastatic myxoid liposarcoma per article title; no direct caption attribution. F: FDG PET with yellow highlight locating myxoid liposarcoma in right atrium and white arrows indicating abdominal metastasis; explicit caption attribution.
panels.attribution_text: Thoddi Ramamurthy et al. Case report: Metastatic myxoid liposarcoma arising from the right atrium extends as cardiac tamponade-A rare case of atrial oncology.. Frontiers in cardiovascular medicine 2022. doi:10.3389/fcvm.2022.1046436. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Lymph node characteristics in the right atrium. (A) CECT thorax revealing minimally enhancing mass lesion in the right atrial wall. (B) Multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes. (C) Horizontal sections of FDG PET scan revealing mildly FDG avid hypodensity (5.8 × 5 cm, SUV max −3.40) along the lateral wall of the right atrium with mass effect over it. (D) Coronal section of FDG PET scan revealing mildly FDG avid mass over the lateral wall of the right atrium. (E) Enlarged FDG avid lymph nodes at perivascular, aortocaval, retrocaval, and bilateral common iliac and external iliac levels (F). Yellow highlighted area locates the myxoid liposarcoma in the right atrium. White arrows in (F) indicates metastasis in abdomen areas.
in_text_mentions: CECT thorax (Figures 2A, B) revealed minimally enhancing mass lesion in the right atrial wall with a small intraluminal component projecting into the right atrial chamber, with multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes. As it was initially suspected to be lymphoma, a PET CT scan (Figures 2C–F) was performed to rule out metastasis, which showed mildly FDG-avid hypodensity along the lateral wall of the right atrium with mass effect over it.

panels.context: Lymph node characteristics in the right atrium. (A) CECT thorax revealing minimally enhancing mass lesion in the right atrial wall. (B) Multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes. (C) Horizontal sections of FDG PET scan revealing mildly FDG avid hypodensity (5.8 × 5 cm, SUV max −3.40) along the lateral wall of the right atrium with mass effect over it. (D) Coronal section of FDG PET scan revealing mildly FDG avid mass over the lateral wall of the right atrium. (E) Enlarged FDG avid lymph nodes at perivascular, aortocaval, retrocaval, and bilateral common iliac and external iliac levels (F). Yellow highlighted area locates the myxoid liposarcoma in the right atrium. White arrows in (F) indicates metastasis in abdomen areas.
